title: Indian Students Are Leaving US Universities in Record Numbers as Visa Rules Tighten
excerpt: With 30,000 students already gone and 70,000 more expected to leave, Germany and Europe emerge as top alternatives as US ends Duration of Status framework.
body:
• Indian student numbers in the US fell to 352,000 in June 2026, down from 382,000 the previous year, with education consultants warning up to 70,000 more could leave in the coming year.
  • Applications from Indian students to US colleges dropped 15% in 2025-26, driven by visa interview delays of 10-11 months, rising costs, and uncertainty over the H-1B pathway.
  • New US visa rules ending the Duration of Status (D/S) system take effect September 15, capping student stays at four years and requiring USCIS extensions — adding bureaucratic hurdles and cost for doctoral students.
  • Germany has emerged as the top alternative, with Indian student numbers doubling from 28,905 in 2023 to 59,400 in 2026. The UK, France, and Netherlands are also gaining ground.

A Sharp Decline in Indian Student Numbers

The American dream is losing its shine for Indian students. According to US study data, Indian student enrollment in American universities fell to 352,000 by June 2026, down 30,000 from 382,000 the previous year. Nearly 30,000 students left the US within a single year without completing their courses, many re-enrolling at European universities instead.

The exodus is accelerating. Education consultants warn that as many as 70,000 more Indian students could leave in the coming year, while Common App data shows applications from Indian students fell 15% during the 2025-26 academic year — part of a broader 10% decline in international applications to US undergraduate programmes.

Visa Delays and Policy Whiplash

Under the current US administration, students are facing visa interview delays of 10 to 11 months, with appointment slots at US embassies and consular offices in India increasingly difficult to secure. The NAFSA Association of International Educators projects that the US economy could lose up to $3.4 billion in direct economic contributions from international students in Fall 2026, with around 40,000 jobs at risk.

A major policy shift compounds the uncertainty. Beginning September 15, the longstanding Duration of Status (D/S) framework — which allowed F-1 visa holders to remain in the US as long as they maintained lawful status — will be replaced by fixed Admit Until Dates. Student stays will be capped at four years or the programme length, whichever is shorter, with a reduced 30-day grace period replacing the previous 60 days.

"Private participation in defined commercial activities can coexist with a strong pathway. What cannot be accepted is a policy that reduces students to perpetual applicants while the cost of education remains in American hands."

— Adapted from education consultant commentary

For doctoral students in science, engineering, or medicine — programmes that routinely run five to seven years — the four-year cap creates an immediate structural problem. A PhD scholar admitted in September 2026 would need to file a formal USCIS extension before their fourth year, adding bureaucratic hurdles, filing fees, and uncertain approval timelines.

The H-1B Cost Shock

The study-to-work pipeline that has long made the US the default choice for Indian students is also under pressure. The Department of Homeland Security has proposed a $103,265 fee for each cap-subject H-1B petition — a figure that could dramatically increase the cost for employers hiring foreign workers and further deter students who plan their education around future US employment.

International applications to US doctoral programmes for Fall 2026 have already fallen 21%, while admissions are projected to decline 17%, according to the Institute of International Education.

Europe Emerges as the Alternative

Germany has been the biggest beneficiary of the shift. Indian student numbers in Germany surged from 28,905 in 2023 to 59,400 in 2026, making Indians the largest international student group in the country — ahead of Chinese students. The UK, France, the Netherlands, Italy, and Spain are also attracting growing interest.

European destinations offer lower tuition costs — with public universities in Germany, France, and the Netherlands often providing free or heavily subsidised education — along with clearer post-study work options, including two-year post-graduation stay permits in several countries. The India-EU mobility framework has further facilitated recognition of Indian qualifications.

Canada, once the other major destination for Indian students, has also seen a dramatic decline. Indian students now account for just 8% of Canada's international student population, down from 52% in 2023, following a 60% drop in international student intake.

What This Means for NRI Families

For diaspora families planning their children's education, the calculus has fundamentally changed. The US still offers unmatched research infrastructure and brand recognition, but the combination of visa uncertainty, rising costs, restrictive H-1B rules, and now the D/S elimination means families must weigh these advantages against more predictable and affordable European alternatives. The decision is no longer automatic — it's a calculation.
